## Summary

Three guests (a former NFL executive, the CEO of a football data company, and the president of the Rams) and an ESPN moderator discuss how NFL front offices have changed. The main threads are why some franchises stay bad, how the GM job has widened into managing many more people, and how analytics gets used when coaches and analysts distrust each other. The guests argue that winning is itself a competitive advantage because it buys time, that analytics works best when built into scouting inputs and not delivered as a separate verdict, and that experience and data should be combined. The talk closes on player load and sleep tracking, AI and virtual reality. Much of it is anecdote from one club and one data vendor.

## Key claims

Caption note: captions carry no speaker labels. Attribution below uses context (the Rams president, the former Patriots executive, the data-company CEO).

- Bill Walsh noted that a handful of plays decide a season, and negative-outlier teams tend to stay the same [01:30].
- The data-company CEO says her company's internal debates split into the scout's experienced eye against what the data shows, and that a cap situation affects supply and demand for a team [02:30] [03:01].
- She says human bias about the "winning formula" shows up as the same mistakes repeated [03:32].
- The former Patriots executive says much of winning and losing comes back to fundamentals such as penalties and turnovers before anything advanced [04:35] [05:06].
- The Rams president says the greatest competitive advantage in sports is winning, because it lets you keep people and refine processes [06:38].
- He says sports has shortened GM time frames and incentivized short-term thinking, and calls building teams "art not science" [07:42] [08:12].
- He says a franchise with established success can make unusual decisions that a struggling franchise could not [08:43].
- He says competitive edges erode quickly because ideas spread among clubs [11:46].
- Moderator: every GM hired since 2022 is under 50 [12:16].
- The former Patriots executive says the biggest change in the GM role is the number of people managed, and the variety of views [13:17] [13:48].
- The Rams president says the Rams split the job into picking players and running the building, and that GMs are rarely trained in leadership or soft skills [14:49] [15:20] [15:52].
- He says failed GMs are not given a second chance the way other executives are [16:53]. The former Patriots executive says several Hall of Fame GMs had rough earlier stints [17:23] [17:56].
- The former Patriots executive says the Patriots kept older, experienced people around [18:26].
- The data-company CEO says her company aims to help GMs work faster with more confidence, for example a trade call answered with history and cap impact in seconds [20:29] [21:00].
- She says an outside vendor can invest over a longer term than a club, including frame-level analytics tied back to film [22:01] [22:33] [23:03].
- The Rams president says analytics works when embedded in scouting profiles before scouts and coaches see them [24:06].
- He says the Rams did not use 40-yard times, used three-cone and other speed measures, and stopped attending the combine five years ago [24:37] [25:08].
- He says trust builds only after two to three years of drafted players succeeding [25:38].
- The former Patriots executive says the hardest part of bringing data to football was insecurity on both sides [26:41] [27:11].
- The Rams president says PFF and similar tools becoming common is "probably for the worst" though it gives cover to ask questions [28:42] [29:12].
- He says a coach may face a fourth-down decision five or six times a year, so a high base rate matters less to that coach [35:49]. He says a decision must be supported with organizational resources to make it work [36:50].
- The former Patriots executive says the largest coaching change he has seen is preparation, including player tracking of load, work and sleep [32:17] [32:47] [33:47].
- The data-company CEO says NFL rules restrict tracking outside the club, and clubs ask players to track sleep for them [37:53].
- On experience versus data: the Rams president says dismissing older or younger staff is a mistake and that debate produces better answers [39:27] [41:29].
- The former Patriots executive says character and leadership are not captured in game tape [42:32].
- Closing: the data-company CEO expects more AI and computer vision, and the panel cites VR preparation for a quarterback and an AI question asked at a retreat [44:35] [45:05] [46:35].

## Numbers and definitions

- Six to ten plays can change a season (Walsh, via the moderator) [01:30].
- 600 years of NFL experience at the data company; the speaker has been in football about eight months [02:30].
- Rams president: 17th year, eight years as a "negative outlier" and eight as a "positive outlier" (his wording) [06:07]; also said 16 years as president [14:18]. Records of three and 13, two and 14, then one and 15 before his arrival and in his early seasons [07:11].
- Scouting budgets: "10 to 15 million do" (caption garbled; probably dollars) per club [11:16].
- Every GM hired since 2022 under 50; of four hired this offseason, two under 40 and one under 35 [12:16]. Unverified; moderator's claim.
- Combine: stopped attending five years ago [25:08].
- Fourth-down base rate "62%" over thousands of plays; the unit (conversion rate or other) is not defined [35:49].
- A 2018 playoff fourth and one, up seven with under eight minutes, is given as an example of a conservative coach going for it [36:19].
- Season length: 16, 17 and "about to be 18" games (as captioned) [32:17].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Analytics baked into scouting profiles and player reviews, so it arrives as an input and not an opinion [24:06].
- Three-cone and other measures of speed used in place of 40 times [24:37].
- Frame-level analytics with probability of events, tied to film; anomaly detection as a prompt to look again [22:33] [23:03].
- Player tracking of load and sleep, limited by league rules [32:17] [37:53].
- A retreat decision run through an AI chatbot; no method is described beyond "asked" (caption: "claw") [46:35].

## Limits and open questions

- No data, sample sizes or outcomes are shown; claims are experience and anecdote.
- The data-company CEO describes her own company's products, and the Rams president describes his club's practices, so these are institutional views.
- The Rams president's own record (eight bad years, eight good) is offered as evidence that winning buys time; it is one club.
- Not using 40 times and skipping the combine are reported without results.
- Captions misspell names (peoli, Lissa, "suer" for the vendor, "Mo rant in", "John idik", "claw") and garble the scouting budget figure.

## Q&A

- Audience question: are older staff stubborn about modern decisions? Answer: dismissing either older or younger people means likely failure; debate is useful [38:54] [39:27].
- Audience question: as analytics grows, does human intuition decline? Answers: character and leadership are not in game tape; combine experience with patterns from data [42:32] [43:02].
- Moderator closing question: what innovation will we be talking about in five years? Answers: AI, computer vision, VR [44:35] [45:05].

## Summary

A closing panel at SSAC25 with two college general managers, one for Stanford football and one for St Bonaventure men's basketball, moderated by an author who says he is here to learn whether there is a book in the subject. The guests describe how their jobs came about, what the job involves, and how college sports money works after NIL and the transfer portal. Topics include a pending legal settlement and a proposed revenue-sharing cap, collectives, recruiting conversations that include money, private equity interest, protecting non-revenue sports, and whether college will "moneyball" teenage recruits. The speakers say the role is still undefined and that they do not know what it will look like in five years.

## Key claims

Caption note: captions carry no speaker labels. Attribution below is "Stanford GM", "St Bonaventure GM" or "moderator" based on context.

- The moderator says the talk is unprepared and he is using it to learn [01:01].
- Stanford GM says he sits atop football and runs it like a pro team president and GM, and believes his is the only structure in college football with a GM above the head coach [02:34].
- He says the university president proposed the role and sees football changing so fast that not keeping up means being left out [03:36] [04:08].
- He had no idea the role would be created; he was seeing GMs appear at other schools, mostly as heads of personnel under a coach [05:10].
- St Bonaventure GM says he is an alum at a school of roughly 1,800 to 1,900 undergraduates, and calls his job "director of survival" [06:11] [07:14].
- He had helped lead the school's collective, then moved to the job from ESPN [08:47] [09:48].
- His job is to serve the coach and players, raise NIL money, build a payroll structure and use his relationships; the coach decides who is on the team [10:50].
- He says his salary cap is a moving target that changes as fundraising changes [12:21]. His recruiting pool is "endless" [13:22].
- Stanford GM says the pending settlement will bring order and a salary cap, and back pay split mostly to football [14:54] [15:26].
- Speakers say collectives will still exist and a third party (Deloitte is named) would police fair market value; deals over a stated threshold must be reported [17:27] [17:57].
- St Bonaventure GM says fair market value numbers are "made up" by everyone and a third party will rule on them [18:59].
- Recruiting conversations include agents, parents and relatives, and include housing asks [20:01] [20:32].
- Stanford GM says admissions has not lowered standards for football or basketball players and that Stanford's plan is to develop high school recruits, not turn over a third of the roster in the portal [21:02] [28:12].
- St Bonaventure GM says his school cannot win bidding wars, so aims to be a first stop for international players, or a place for players who need a reset, and plans a roster of players 25 and under [24:38] [25:08] [27:10].
- He builds relationships with top high school players who may come back via the portal in two or three years [25:39].
- He treats his cap like an NBA cap, with percentages for top players, mid-level and minimums [27:41].
- Both say replacing a player is typically more expensive than keeping him [29:44].
- Collectives have contracts with players, but players are in effect free agents each year; the extent to which schools can walk away is unknown [30:14] [30:44].
- Stanford GM says football leads revenue and realignment, and supports funding Olympic sports; there is no athletic director at Stanford now, so the president will arbitrate [31:15] [32:46].
- Both say private equity conversations are happening; the speakers mention a conference-level deal in the Big 12 (caption: "Red Bird") [33:17] [34:18].
- Both argue for keeping the student-athlete idea, and St Bonaventure GM says basketball competitiveness is existential for the school [35:48] [36:48].
- Stanford GM says the head coach's job has grown untenable for one person, which is why college teams resemble pro teams [40:26].
- Stanford GM says data science will be applied to evaluating teenage recruits, with greater financial incentive to get it right [40:57] [41:27].
- Both say team-first players and a fit with the program handle unequal pay [42:29] [43:01] [43:31].
- Both say they still do not know what their jobs will be, only that they will need more money [43:31] [44:34].

## Numbers and definitions

- Proposed cap: the captions give "$25 million" [14:24], then "$2.5 million" [14:54], then "$20.5 million" [15:26], and "$20 million" as a hypothetical [31:15]. The captions are garbled; the likely figure is about 20.5 million across all sports, but this is an inference from captions and not stated cleanly. Do not use any of these figures.
- Back pay split: "75% money going to football players 15% men's basketball 5% women's basketball 5" (captions; the last part is garbled) [15:26].
- Reporting threshold for NIL deals: "$600" (as captioned) [17:57].
- St Bonaventure: 12 of the last 20 games won against Power four and Big East teams (as captioned; unclear if "Power four" is the speaker's exact term) [07:44].
- Ex-salary comparison: "$7 million" to "$70,000" job, referring to an ESPN article the moderator read [05:41]. This is the moderator's claim, not verified.
- A $10 million Michigan quarterback figure is called "allegedly" [23:06].
- Stanford: 36 sports; "59 current in in alums" at the Olympics (garbled in captions) [32:15].
- Rough figure for helping a player reach a high major: "a million and a half two million dollars a year" [25:08].
- Settlement date: "April 7th something like that April 8th" [14:54]. Speaker unsure.

## Methods and frameworks named

- NBA salary-cap framing applied to an NIL budget: top-heavy payroll, mid-level, minimum [27:41].
- Recruiting by relationship and trust in chosen regions, not broad coverage [13:22].
- Developing high school players for four years versus an older, portal-heavy roster [27:10] [28:12].
- Third-party review of NIL deals for fair market value [17:57].

## Limits and open questions

- The moderator says he is learning and the session is unprepared; there are no datasets, and all claims are the speakers' own views.
- Both guests speak for their schools; the Stanford GM has a university interest in keeping academic standards and the student-athlete model.
- The settlement, cap and oversight details were pending and unclear to the speakers themselves.
- Only two schools in two sports; neither resembles a large conference football program in budget or recruiting pool.
- Cap, back pay and other money figures are garbled in the captions.
- Who decides how funds are split between football and other sports is left open [32:46].

## Q&A

- Moderator: what do recruiting money conversations sound like? Answers: a spectrum from agents to parents; housing is part of it [20:01] [20:32].
- Audience question read by the moderator: how do players relate when one is paid much more than teammates? Answers: locker rooms know who the best players are; team-first fit matters [41:58] [42:29] [43:31].
- Moderator closing: will your jobs be different in five years? Answers: neither knows; more money will be needed [43:31] [44:34].
